title: What Nobody Tells You After Graduation
author: Jonathan Boymal
summary: Boymal offers reflective advice for graduates entering professional life, where the scaffolding of courses and rubrics suddenly disappears. He argues that professional life arrives through small ordinary acts, and that readiness is built by beginning rather than waiting for certainty. He urges intellectual humility, learning through relationships and legitimate peripheral participation, and regular reflection so one does not drift into the normalized harms of respectable work. The practical section covers attention management, keeping commitments, upward management as stewardship, situational awareness, curiosity, empowering others and kindness toward oneself. He closes by asking readers to know their strengths and values and to keep starting again. The unifying move is to treat early career as a formation of character and judgment, not a hunt for the perfect role.
points: The transition out of structured education demands self-directed orientation: you cannot wait to feel ready, and your convictions should be held with care but lightly.
Workplaces teach through social learning and 'hot cognition', meaning reading emotion and context, which universities seldom train.
Trust is built through small signals such as honouring even minor commitments and showing up without obligation.
Upward management means bringing options rather than problems, clarifying what success looks like and reading the room with situational awareness.
Reflection with regular check-ups and a clear sense of personal values protects against building a life that looks good but feels hollow.
quotes: There’s a strange moment in life that comes just after you graduate, one that nobody quite prepares you for. You’ve spent years in an environment with clear expectations, goals, and feedback.

Try not to grip too tightly to any one identity or idea of what you’re “meant” to be. Hold your convictions with care, but lightly, allowing them to evolve in the presence of new evidence, new perspectives and new realities.

University often emphasises cold cognition: focused, abstract, and solitary problem-solving. But in the workplace, hot cognition matters just as much: responding in real time, reading emotion and context, staying attuned to others.
Show up and honour your commitments, even the small ones. People notice when you’re there without obligation or obvious benefit. These gestures build quiet trust.
Learn the art of upward management as a form of stewardship. Respect your manager’s time by offering options and solutions, not just problems.
And cultivate situational awareness - the ability to read a room, know when to speak and when to stay quiet, when to follow norms and when to break them.
Learn to ask the questions that matter, not just those that have tidy answers. Be curious about what people value, what motivates them, what they’re struggling with. This is empathy in action.
